title: A Figure in Open Space
question: What changes when a figure has room around it?
thesis: Begin with small or loosely bounded figures, follow the space around their bodies, and close with a figure that nearly fills its setting. Focus on scale, placement and the surrounding field.

title: Characters in Silhouette
question: How much can a solid shape tell us?
thesis: Follow characters built from dark silhouettes and small facial signs. Move from reduced shapes to figures with surrounding waves or interior marks; let a more layered figure complicate the apparent simplicity.

title: The Body Makes a Gesture
question: Where does movement begin in a still drawing?
thesis: Follow leaning bodies, raised hands, outstretched limbs and changes of stance. Contrast the direction of a pose with the direction of the surrounding brush marks without attributing a motive to the figure.

title: Figures in Company
question: When do separate figures begin to form a group?
thesis: Begin with distinct figures sharing a field; move toward paired and grouped bodies whose outlines overlap. Use the spacing between figures and the lines connecting them to frame differences in their relationships.

title: Finding Faces in a Crowd
question: What lets one face emerge from a crowded drawing?
thesis: Follow heads and figures within crowded, crossed compositions. Open with recognizable characters, move through ambiguous shared outlines, and close with a drawing where a visitor can find several different points of entry.

title: Characters Beyond the Human Face
question: What makes a shape read as a character?
thesis: Follow animal-like bodies, creature-like forms and objects that acquire facial signs. Contrast recognizable silhouettes with less certain characters; describe visible forms without treating inferred species or objects as facts.

title: Figures, Places and Light
question: When does the surrounding space become part of the subject?
thesis: Look at setting, cast shadow, beams, landscape-like structures and changes of ground. Let the surroundings redirect attention away from the face while keeping uncertain scene readings explicitly open.

title: Letters Among the Marks
question: How does a readable sign change the way we look?
thesis: Begin with recognizable lettering or emblems, then examine how they share a surface with bodies and brush marks. Contrast readable text with signs that behave as shapes; do not invent the meaning of a symbol.

title: Lines Moving Outward
question: How do marks carry a figure into its surroundings?
thesis: Follow rays, spokes, waves and spikes spreading from a central form. Compare orderly repetition with loose directional lines and a closing work whose center becomes harder to locate.

title: Across the Surface
question: What do bands and repeated marks hold together?
thesis: Follow horizontal bands, zigzag rows, grids and recurring units as they divide or connect an image. Move between recognizable heads and compositions where pattern competes with the figure.

title: Looking into Circles
question: When is a circle an eye, and when is it a pattern?
thesis: Follow coiled eyes, rounded sockets and repeated circular forms. Compare circles that fix a gaze with circles that spread across the image; let a less clearly facial work reopen the question.

title: Two Sides of a Face
question: How does a face hold together when its two sides differ?
thesis: Follow mismatched eyes, split color areas and unequal facial structures. Contrast slight differences with more divided heads, keeping emotional readings grounded in the visible imbalance rather than diagnosing a figure.

title: The Shape of a Mouth
question: How do similar teeth leave an expression unresolved?
thesis: Compare mouth openings, repeated teeth, lips and jaw shapes across otherwise different heads. Move between possible grins and grimaces without fixing an emotion; use construction and spacing to explain the contrast.

title: Heads Emerging from Darkness
question: Which marks let a face become visible against a dark ground?
thesis: Follow highlights, colored crossings and layered heads on dark fields. Begin with a legible outline, move through shadowed features, and close with a head whose boundary is difficult to keep separate from the surrounding marks.

title: Building the Head
question: What gives a drawn head its structure?
thesis: Follow rectangular scaffolding, broad color areas and modeled volumes. Compare flat stacked features with rounded heads, and close with a work whose surface marks pull against its apparent solidity.
